extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, comedians, linguists and anyone interested in humor/word-based wit
extracted.subtask_description: A taxonomy and descriptive guide to forms of wordplay — techniques that use words themselves as the primary vehicle for humor or effect, with examples and related phenomena. Useful for writers, comedians, puzzle-makers, and translators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay (general / play-on-words)
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary technique and form of wit in which words used become the main subject of the work, primarily for intended effect or amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include puns, phonetic mix-ups (spoonerisms), obscure words and meanings, rhetorical excursions, oddly formed sentences, double entendres, and telling character names. Wordplay is common in oral cultures and appears in both alphabetic and non-alphabetic writing systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tom Swifties
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of humorous writing where adverbs are chosen to reflect the nature of the situation in a punning way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Hurry up and get to the back of the ship,' Tom said sternly. Use an adverb that creates a pun or semantic echo with the quoted sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wellerisms
rubrics_metrics.description: A device using linguistic fossils and set phrases, often a saying followed by a humorous or literal tag identifying the speaker or circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'We'll have to rehearse that,' said the undertaker as the coffin fell out of the car. Structure typically: proverb/wise saying + unexpected literalizing attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpaired words
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate use of unusual or obsolete antonyms or forms, e.g., back-formation from a common word to create an odd counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I was well-coiffed and sheveled' (back-formation from 'disheveled'). Use rare or archaic forms to create surprise or comic mismatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoonerism
rubrics_metrics.description: An accidental (or deliberate) and often humorous transposition of initial letters or sounds between words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a flock of bats' instead of 'a block of flats' or 'a bunny phone' instead of 'a funny bone'. Often used for phonetic play or comic slips of the tongue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malapropism
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing a word with a different word that sounds similar, either unintentionally or for comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'He is the very pineapple of politeness.' (instead of 'pinnacle'). Use near-homophones or similar-sounding words to create absurd meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthimeria
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering a word's regular part of speech (e.g., using a noun as a verb) for emphasis or comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The thunder would not peace at my bidding' (using 'peace' as a verb), or 'The little old lady turtled across the street.' Can reflect natural language change or deliberate stylistic play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double entendre
rubrics_metrics.description: Using words or phrases with multiple meanings ambiguously, often producing a humorous or sexual effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mae West's 'Marriage is a fine institution, but I'm not ready for an institution.' and Groucho Marx's 'If I said you had a beautiful body, would you hold it against me?' Rely on layered senses for comedic ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portmanteau
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining two words to create a new word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'smog' from 'smoke' + 'fog'. Useful for concise novel coinages that capture blended concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling character names
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing character names that themselves are plays on words or have punning significance relative to the character or theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Importance of Being Earnest — the name 'Ernest' sounding like 'earnest'. Use names to signal traits, irony, or thematic wordplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthographic and phonetic (text-based) wordplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordplay that exploits written form or phonetics, found in languages with or without alphabet-based scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes homophonic puns (e.g., in Mandarin), visual letterplay where letter shapes convey meaning, and bilingual orthographic tricks. Useful for signage, logos, and multilingual contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branding / business-name wordplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Using wordplay to make business or product names more memorable or culturally resonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a business near the UN Headquarters playing on 'UN Peacekeepers' in its name; bilingual signs that exploit letter shapes. Consider cultural/regional differences and legibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crossword and puzzle-oriented wordplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordplay employed structurally in puzzles; cryptic crosswords are especially based on elaborate systems of wordplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use definitions, anagrams, homophones, hidden words and other conventional cryptic devices. Wordplay here must balance solvability and cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedicated wordplay authorship / stylistic commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a writer makes wordplay a central feature of their work (some authors are particularly committed or adept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Shakespeare's 'quibbles', P. G. Wodehouse's comic wordplay, James Joyce's dense wordplay in Finnegans Wake. Consider consistency, range, and depth of play when evaluating an author's use of wordplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay as source of neologisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordplay can enter common usage, producing new words or senses (neologisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portmanteaus and playful coinages may become standard terms over time (e.g., 'smog'). Assess uptake and semantic transparency when considering lasting effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translatability and cross-linguistic constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordplay often causes problems for translators because language-specific sounds, meanings, or orthographic coincidences may not transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a pun in Winnie-the-Pooh that depends on English homophony disappears in translation. When creating wordplay intended for multilingual audiences, account for loss of pun, consider cultural substitutions, or provide explanatory strategies.
